$$\int \overline{\varphi_i(x)} \varphi_j(x) dx = \delta_{ij} \tag{2}$$

and real numbers $\varepsilon_1, \ldots, \varepsilon_N$ .

# Session 76. Fetch/read step only. NOTHING BELOW IS A RULING.
# No sealed file edited. c = 137.035999 unchanged. 107 rows, Z=2..108.

## WHAT WAS ASKED
PLAN-PROOF-ROUTES.md STEP 0: make Φ a mathematical object.
  (i)   existence of the HF minimiser
  (ii)  SCF fixed point — uniqueness or a stated selection rule
  (iii) uniqueness of the argmin

## F76.1 · THE PLAN NAMED THE WRONG THEOREM FOR THE ANSATZ Φ USES.
SEVERITY: RECORD-AND-CORRECT. TOUCHES NO SCORED ROW. RAISED BY ME, AT FETCH.
The plan asserts "Lieb-Simon 1977: minimisers exist for N <= Z", carried as the
authority for Step 0(i). **Lieb-Simon 1977 is GENERAL Hartree-Fock (GHF): no
constraint but orthonormality, condition Z > N-1.** Φ's §3 ansatz is NOT GHF. It
fixes one radial function per (n,l) channel, spherical harmonics, spin factorised:
    phi_{jm,sigma} = (f_j(r)/r) Y_{l_j m} delta_{sigma,mu}
That is the RESTRICTED (RHF) functional. **The gap is stated in the literature in
so many words:** Lieb and Simon extend GHF to certain restricted cases in
J. Chem. Phys. 61 (1974) 735, "but their theorem does not cover the restrictions
discussed in this paper" (Hantsch, arXiv:1206.4932, §1).
**CITING LIEB-SIMON FOR Φ WOULD HAVE BEEN AN AUDIT BY NAME — R-A's own fault
shape, applied to a citation instead of a lever.**

## STEP 0(i) — EXISTENCE. SETTLED, AND BY A STRONGER THEOREM THAN THE ONE PLANNED.
**F. Hantsch, "Existence of Minimizers in Restricted Hartree-Fock Theory",
arXiv:1206.4932, Theorem 2.1.** OPEN ACCESS, PRIMARY, READ IN FULL THIS SESSION.
Its RHF functional (5) is built from orbitals of exactly Φ's form (3), with
prescribed angular momentum quantum numbers l_1..l_s0.
  * A minimiser exists for the relaxed problem for ALL Z > 0.
  * (ii) If Z >= N-1, then ||f_i|| = 1 for every shell.
  * (iii) If Z > N-1, then additionally eps_i < 0 for every shell.
**EVERY SCORED ROW IS A NEUTRAL ATOM, N = Z, hence Z = N > N-1 STRICTLY.** All 107
rows sit inside case (iii) — normalised minimiser, all shell eigenvalues bound.
Not on the boundary; not in the open case Z = N-1.

## AND AN INDEPENDENT WITNESS TO §3 THAT WE DID NOT HAVE.
Hantsch §4 derives the RHF functional from the GHF functional and obtains the
exchange kernel
    U_{l l'}(r,s) = SUM_k (l l' k; 000)^2 * min{r,s}^k / max{r,s}^{k+1}
**This is §3's c_k = (l_a k l_b; 000)^2 and Y^k_ab, in a published derivation that
has never seen this project.** §3's DERIVED label on the Euler-Lagrange equations
and the angular coefficients now has an external, primary witness. The radial Fock
operator of his (7), H_l = -d^2/dr^2 + l(l+1)/r^2 - Z/r + 2U - K_l, is §3's
operator. **This is the first time an outside source has independently written down
the object Φ solves.**

## STEP 0(ii) — SCF FIXED POINT. UNIQUENESS IS NOT AVAILABLE. A SELECTION RULE IS
## REQUIRED, AND THE LITERATURE FORBIDS ASSUMING OTHERWISE.
  * **P.-L. Lions, CMP 109 (1987) 33-97:** there exists a SEQUENCE of solutions to
    the HF equations. Critical points are not unique in general.
  * **Griesemer & Hantsch, ARMA 203 (2012) 883-900 (arXiv:1012.5179):** the HF
    ground state of a CLOSED SHELL atom is unique provided Z is sufficiently large
    COMPARED TO N — for two electrons, Z >= 35. **They give an example showing
    Z > N-1 is NOT sufficient in general, and report phase segregation at some
    Z > 1.**
**CONSEQUENCE FOR US, STATED AGAINST US: our rows are neutral (Z = N), which is the
OPPOSITE of the Z >> N regime where uniqueness is proved, and most of them are open
shell, which is outside the closed-shell hypothesis entirely. STEP 0(ii) CANNOT BE
CLOSED BY UNIQUENESS. It must be closed by a STATED SELECTION RULE.**
The convergence ladder (beta, maxit) is today a numerical control. Relevant prior
art for what it is: Cances & Le Bris, M2AN 34 (2000) 749-774, convergence of SCF
algorithms; Levitt, M2AN 46 (2012) 1321-1336, gradient-based algorithms. These
prove convergence TO A CRITICAL POINT. **They do not say WHICH.**

## STEP 0(iii) — UNIQUENESS OF THE ARGMIN. TWO SEPARATE OBJECTS, DO NOT CONFLATE.
  * **The aufbau principle as a theorem exists — in the WRONG theory.** Bach, Lieb,
    Loss & Solovej, PRL 72 (1994) 2981, "There Are No Unfilled Shells in Unrestricted
    Hartree-Fock Theory": occupied orbitals are the N lowest eigenvalues of the Fock
    operator, with a gap to the unoccupied. **Hantsch's Remark (b) to Thm 2.1 records
    that it is NOT KNOWN whether this holds in RESTRICTED HF, and that the method of
    that proof is not applicable there.** The nearest mathematical form of "the
    aufbau principle" is a theorem in UHF and OPEN in the theory Φ inhabits.
  * **BUT Φ DOES NOT SELECT BY EIGENVALUE ORDER.** §3 step 3 selects the argmin of a
    TOTAL-ENERGY difference over admissible channels. The BLLS gap theorem is
    therefore not the lemma Φ needs, and the open RHF question is not a hole beneath
    Φ. **Φ's requirement is weaker and finite: at each Z, that the argmin over a
    finite candidate set is attained once.** That is decidable row by row and is
    MEASURABLE — it is the margin column we already own.
  * NOTED AGAINST US: Lions' treatment of the restricted equations rests on the
    unproven assertion that all eigenvalues of a radial Fock operator are simple.
    **We must not import that assertion.**

## WHAT IS NOW OPEN AT STEP 0, PRECISELY
  A. A written selection rule for the SCF fixed point, replacing (beta, maxit) as a
     numerical control. NOT closed by uniqueness; uniqueness is false in our regime.
  B. Uniqueness of the argmin at all 107 rows — the min gap between winner and
     runner-up, measured, not recalled. NOT YET RUN THIS SESSION.
  C. Whether the candidate set of §3 step 1 is a definable object independent of the
     program. Route A already flags the truncation as sampled, not proved.

## PROVENANCE
arXiv:1206.4932 fetched and read in full. arXiv:1012.5179 abstract + intro read.
**Project Euclid (CMP 53, 185-194) was NOT reachable: blocked by bot protection,
NOT a paywall. Lieb-Simon 1977 remains UNREAD IN PRIMARY FORM by this project and
must be labelled [SECONDARY] exactly as A1 is — but it is no longer load-bearing,
because Hantsch Thm 2.1 replaces it.**
EOF

**SESSION 76 — THREE SEGMENTS CLOSED. STEP 0 IS NOW (i) SETTLED, (ii) DRAFTED, (iii) MEASURED.**

**§1 · AMENDED — `pack76/AMENDMENT-F76.1.md`**
Step 0(i) authority replaced with Hantsch Thm 2.1 (restricted HF, Φ's exact ansatz). Lieb–Simon 1977 demoted to `[SECONDARY]`, load-bearing for nothing. Provenance corrected and kept separate from A1: Project Euclid was **bot-blocked, not paywalled**, and the two unread papers must never be reported as one condition. The amendment extends R-A: **a citation by name is not a citation — hypotheses must be matched to the object, term by term.**

**§2 · SELECTION RULE — `pack76/POSITION-S76-SELECTION-RULE.md`**
Prior art exists and it states our gap in its own words. Griesemer and Hantsch record that while convergence analysis of SCF algorithms has advanced, it remains poorly understood what is actually being approximated; that the Hartree–Fock functional for a neutral atom has a minimiser and infinitely many other critical points; that uniqueness is unproven even where expected; and that it is not known whether different methods reach different critical points.

The rule I propose is variational, not algorithmic: **the field is a global minimiser of E^RHF at the candidate's fixed occupancies**, over Hantsch's relaxed set — where the relaxation is free (E = Ẽ) and existence is Theorem 2.1. **(β, maxit) then leaves the definition entirely.** That is what Step 0 asked for.

It creates a real obligation, and I name it rather than bury it: convergence theorems deliver *a critical point only*, so **Route C must show the program reaches the global minimiser.** Our three-seed basin test (TFD/Latter/α=2/3 agreeing to 0.005 mHa from 52 Ha away) is the right kind of evidence and **is not a proof of a global minimum.** Drafted, not derived, not adopted — awaiting your ruling.

**§3 · MEASURED — `pack76/RESULT-S76-ARGMIN.md`** (prediction hashed first, R 1449)

- **Exact ties: 0 of 107.** The argmin is attained once at every scored row.
- **Tightest margin 32.330 mHa at Z=89 (6d over 7p)** — 646× the 0.05 mHa floor. Median 207 mHa.
- Margin column verified against the ranked list it derives from: **107/107, zero disagreements.**

**And the flag I set against myself fired.** P4 predicted the per-row argmin margin would *not* be identical to the 32.33 mHa the ledger already owned, and stated that equality would mean I had re-read a column rather than measured one. **They are equal to the digit.** Step 0(iii)'s central number was already owned; I report this as a re-read. What is genuinely new is small: ties excluded by measurement, the column cross-checked, and the runner-up identities — at Z=89 the runner-up is **7p, not 5f**, so the contest actinium loses is not the one the tie-break story names.

P5 also failed, usefully: margins do **not** narrow with Z — Z=104 and Z=103 are the widest after helium. **Tight rows are where channels cross, not where Z is large.**

**§4 · CONTEXT** — approx. 72%. Handoff not yet required; I will state at 90%.

**§5 · WHAT STEP 0 STILL OWES**
Only one item is genuinely open: **adoption of the selection rule**, plus the falsifier it implies — perturb a converged solution and re-converge; a lower second basin kills the rule as stated. That is cheap and not yet run.

Route A's target is now sharper: certified enclosure width must come in **strictly under 32.330 mHa**, and the candidate set is not fixed in size (3 to 13 across rows), so truncation still needs proving rather than sampling.

## Abstract

Symmetry-projected Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov (HFB) equations are derived using the variational ansatz for the generalized one-body density-matrix in the Valatin form. It is shown that the projected-energy functional can be completely expressed in terms of the HFB density-matrix and the pairing-tensor. # Variations of the Hartree-Fock fractional-spin error for one electron

Hugh G. A. Burton, 1, a) Clotilde Marut, 2 Timothy J. Daas, 3 Paola Gori-Giorgi, 3 and Pierre-François Loos 2, b)

Fractional-spin errors are inherent in all current approximate density functionals, including Hartree–Fock theory, and their origin has been related to strong static correlation effects. The conventional way to encode fractional-spin calculations is to construct an ensemble density that scales between the high-spin and low-spin densities. In this article, we explore the variation of the Hartree–Fock fractional-spin (or ghost-interaction) error in one-electron systems using restricted and unrestricted ensemble densities, and the exact generalized Hartree–Fock representation. By considering the hydrogen atom and  $H_2^+$  cation, we analyze how the unrestricted and generalized Hartree–Fock schemes minimize this error by localizing the electrons or rotating the spin coordinates. 

the structure of an approximate density or wave function.<sup>16</sup> This analysis relies on the idea that a well separated fragment of a pure-state system might be locally described as an ensemble, and that it should be correctly described in this way by an energy functional (for an in-depth critical analysis, see Refs. 38 and 39). Furthermore, these errors can be directly connected to the ghost interaction between different states in an ensemble density calculation.<sup>40</sup>

While the relationship between fractional-spin errors and static correlation are now well established, the corresponding short-comings of the exchange-correlation functional remain elusive. Hartree–Fock theory does not satisfy the fractionalspin condition, suggesting that artificial Coulomb interactions play a significant role.

In the simplest case the state of the electrons is described by a single Slater determinant and one seeks to minimize the energy by variation of the one-electron orbitals. This is done by some self-consistent field algorithm such as the Roothaan, or the level-shift algorithm [5]. While there has been remarkable progress recently in the analysis of convergence properties of these algorithms [5, 4], it is still poorly understood what is actually being approximated. To some extent this is due to our ignorance about the set of critical points of the Hartree-Fock functional: we know that the Hartree-Fock functional for a neutral atom has a minimizer and infinitely many other critical points [16, 17], but uniqueness of the minimizer, e.g., is not known even in cases where it is expected. Neither is it known whether distinct methods for finding critical points lead to distinct critical points. Our goal is to give answers to such questions.

# POSITION S76 — THE SCF SELECTION RULE. STEP 0(ii).
# M's ruling s76 item 2: identify and derive the selection rule; check prior art first.
# THIS IS A POSITION, NOT A RULING AND NOT A RESULT.

## 1 · THE PROBLEM IS NAMED IN THE LITERATURE, IN THE LITERATURE'S OWN WORDS.
Griesemer & Hantsch, arXiv:1012.5179 §1, on the state of the field:
  * SCF algorithms (Roothaan, level-shift) are what is actually run;
  * convergence analysis has advanced, **but it is still poorly understood WHAT IS
    BEING APPROXIMATED**;
  * the HF functional for a NEUTRAL ATOM has a minimiser **and infinitely many other
    critical points**;
  * uniqueness of the minimiser is not known even where it is expected;
  * **it is not known whether distinct methods for finding critical points lead to
    distinct critical points.**
**THAT IS STEP 0(ii) VERBATIM, POSED BY THE FIELD AND OPEN THERE. We are not
discovering a private difficulty and we must not report it as one.**

## 2 · THE PRIOR ART THAT SUPPLIES THE SHAPE OF A RULE.
**Lieb's variational principle (relaxation from projections to 0 <= gamma <= 1)** is
the standard device: the infimum over the relaxed convex set equals the infimum over
rank-N projections, so the minimiser is characterised VARIATIONALLY rather than by
whatever the algorithm converges to. Review: V. Bach, "Hartree-Fock Theory, Lieb's
Variational Principle, and their Generalizations", arXiv:2209.10189.
**THE RESTRICTED ANALOGUE IS ALREADY IN OUR HAND AND IS THE ONE THAT APPLIES.**
Hantsch arXiv:1206.4932 Remark (c) to (6): the orthonormality constraints may be
relaxed to <f_i,f_j> = 0 for l_i = l_j, i != j and ||f_i|| <= 1 **WITHOUT LOWERING
THE GROUND STATE ENERGY** — E(N,Z) = Etilde(N,Z) — and Theorem 2.1 produces a
minimiser of the relaxed problem, which at Z > N-1 is normalised with every
eps_i < 0. **The relaxed problem has a minimiser; the relaxation is free.**

## 3 · THE RULE PROPOSED, IN THE FORM STEP 0 REQUIRES.
> **SELECTION RULE (PROPOSED).** For each Z and each candidate channel, the field is
> defined to be **a global minimiser of the restricted Hartree-Fock functional
> E^RHF at the fixed shell occupancies of that candidate**, over the relaxed set of
> Hantsch (8). Existence: Hantsch Theorem 2.1. Every scored row satisfies Z > N-1,
> so the minimiser is normalised with all shell eigenvalues strictly bound.
**WHAT THIS BUYS:** Φ is then defined by a VARIATIONAL PROPERTY, not by a trajectory.
**(beta, maxit) LEAVES THE DEFINITION ENTIRELY** and becomes what it always was — a
numerical scheme for approaching an independently defined object. That is exactly
what Step 0 asked for.
**WHAT IT DOES NOT BUY:** it does not make the minimiser unique. It does not have to.
A selection rule needs to name ONE object, not prove there is only one candidate.

## 4 · THE OBLIGATION THIS CREATES, AND IT IS A REAL ONE.
Defining Φ by the global minimiser transfers the burden to the code:
**THE PROGRAM MUST BE SHOWN TO REACH THE GLOBAL MINIMISER AND NOT A SADDLE OR A
LOCAL ONE.** Convergence theorems (Cances & Le Bris M2AN 34 (2000) 749; Levitt M2AN
46 (2012) 1321) deliver A CRITICAL POINT ONLY. **This obligation belongs to ROUTE C
and it is now load-bearing there, where before it was not named.**
**EVIDENCE WE ALREADY HOLD, AND ITS EXACT WEIGHT:** the seed study — TFD, Latter,
alpha = 2/3 — agrees to **0.005 mHa from 52 Ha away**. That is a THREE-START BASIN
TEST and it is the right kind of evidence. **THREE STARTS IS NOT A PROOF OF A GLOBAL
MINIMUM AND MUST NOT BE QUOTED AS ONE.** The falsifier is cheap and is not yet run:
perturb the converged solution and re-converge; a second basin at lower energy kills
the rule as stated.

## 5 · A WARNING CARRIED FROM THE READING.
Lions' treatment of the RESTRICTED equations relies on the unproven assertion that
all eigenvalues of a radial Fock operator are simple. **We do not import it.** Our
rule is stated on the ENERGY, not on the spectrum, precisely to avoid needing it.

Griesemer & Hantsch, arXiv:1012.5179 §1, on the state of the field:
  * SCF algorithms (Roothaan, level-shift) are what is actually run;
  * convergence analysis has advanced, **but it is still poorly understood WHAT IS
    BEING APPROXIMATED**;
  * the HF functional for a NEUTRAL ATOM has a minimiser **and infinitely many other
    critical points**;
  * uniqueness of the minimiser is not known even where it is expected;
  * **it is not known whether distinct methods for finding critical points lead to
    distinct critical points.**
**THAT IS STEP 0(ii) VERBATIM, POSED BY THE FIELD AND OPEN THERE. We are not
discovering a private difficulty and we must not report it as one.**

## 2 · THE PRIOR ART THAT SUPPLIES THE SHAPE OF A RULE.
**Lieb's variational principle (relaxation from projections to 0 <= gamma <= 1)** is
the standard device: the infimum over the relaxed convex set equals the infimum over
rank-N projections, so the minimiser is characterised VARIATIONALLY rather than by
whatever the algorithm converges to. Review: V. Bach, "Hartree-Fock Theory, Lieb's
Variational Principle, and their Generalizations", arXiv:2209.10189.
**THE RESTRICTED ANALOGUE IS ALREADY IN OUR HAND AND IS THE ONE THAT APPLIES.**
Hantsch arXiv:1206.4932 Remark (c) to (6): the orthonormality constraints may be
relaxed to <f_i,f_j> = 0 for l_i = l_j, i != j and ||f_i|| <= 1 **WITHOUT LOWERING
THE GROUND STATE ENERGY** — E(N,Z) = Etilde(N,Z) — and Theorem 2.1 produces a
minimiser of the relaxed problem, which at Z > N-1 is normalised with every
eps_i < 0. **The relaxed problem has a minimiser; the relaxation is free.**

## 3 · THE RULE PROPOSED, IN THE FORM STEP 0 REQUIRES.
> **SELECTION RULE (PROPOSED).** For each Z and each candidate channel, the field is
> defined to be **a global minimiser of the restricted Hartree-Fock functional
> E^RHF at the fixed shell occupancies of that candidate**, over the relaxed set of
> Hantsch (8). Existence: Hantsch Theorem 2.1. Every scored row satisfies Z > N-1,
> so the minimiser is normalised with all shell eigenvalues strictly bound.
**WHAT THIS BUYS:** Φ is then defined by a VARIATIONAL PROPERTY, not by a trajectory.
**(beta, maxit) LEAVES THE DEFINITION ENTIRELY** and becomes what it always was — a
numerical scheme for approaching an independently defined object. That is exactly
what Step 0 asked for.
**WHAT IT DOES NOT BUY:** it does not make the minimiser unique. It does not have to.
A selection rule needs to name ONE object, not prove there is only one candidate.

Defining Φ by the global minimiser transfers the burden to the code:
**THE PROGRAM MUST BE SHOWN TO REACH THE GLOBAL MINIMISER AND NOT A SADDLE OR A
LOCAL ONE.** Convergence theorems (Cances & Le Bris M2AN 34 (2000) 749; Levitt M2AN
46 (2012) 1321) deliver A CRITICAL POINT ONLY. **This obligation belongs to ROUTE C
and it is now load-bearing there, where before it was not named.**

the rule as stated.

Step 0(i) authority replaced with Hantsch Thm 2.1 (restricted HF, Φ's exact ansatz). Lieb–Simon 1977 demoted to `[SECONDARY]`, load-bearing for nothing. Provenance corrected and kept separate from A1: Project Euclid was **bot-blocked, not paywalled**, and the two unread papers must never be reported as one condition. The amendment extends R-A: **a citation by name is not a citation — hypotheses must be matched to the object, term by term.**

**§2 · SELECTION RULE — `pack76/POSITION-S76-SELECTION-RULE.md`**
Prior art exists and it states our gap in its own words. Griesemer and Hantsch record that while convergence analysis of SCF algorithms has advanced, it remains poorly understood what is actually being approximated; that the Hartree–Fock functional for a neutral atom has a minimiser and infinitely many other critical points; that uniqueness is unproven even where expected; and that it is not known whether different methods reach different critical points.

The rule I propose is variational, not algorithmic: **the field is a global minimiser of E^RHF at the candidate's fixed occupancies**, over Hantsch's relaxed set — where the relaxation is free (E = Ẽ) and existence is Theorem 2.1. **(β, maxit) then leaves the definition entirely.** That is what Step 0 asked for.

It creates a real obligation, and I name it rather than bury it: convergence theorems deliver *a critical point only*, so **Route C must show the program reaches the global minimiser.** Our three-seed basin test (TFD/Latter/α=2/3 agreeing to 0.005 mHa from 52 Ha away) is the right kind of evidence and **is not a proof of a global minimum.** Drafted, not derived, not adopted — awaiting your ruling.

**And the flag I set against myself fired.** P4 predicted the per-row argmin margin would *not* be identical to the 32.33 mHa the ledger already owned, and stated that equality would mean I had re-read a column rather than measured one. **They are equal to the digit.** Step 0(iii)'s central number was already owned; I report this as a re-read. What is genuinely new is small: ties excluded by measurement, the column cross-checked, and the runner-up identities — at Z=89 the runner-up is **7p, not 5f**, so the contest actinium loses is not the one the tie-break story names.

P5 also failed, usefully: margins do **not** narrow with Z — Z=104 and Z=103 are the widest after helium. **Tight rows are where channels cross, not where Z is large.**

**§1 · THE LANGUAGE THE PROJECT ALREADY OWNS FOR THIS OBJECT**
The Method's §D.4.4 describes a structure exactly congruent to SCF: **many presentations map to one normal form; the map forgets which one was used, and the forgetting is not recoverable.** Λ → recovered bounds is a function; the inverse is not.

That is the SCF map. Griesemer–Hantsch ask "what is actually being approximated" — the project's own answer in a different language is: **an idempotent closure, whose value is well-defined and whose pre-image is not.** And the Method adds the part the HF literature does not say: *a presentation carries structure the object does not.* The starting field carries information the converged field has destroyed. **The right question is not "which critical point" but "what does the map forget, and does the retained part decide the answer."** That reframing is transferable to future researchers as-is.

**§2 · WHAT WE CAN HAND THEM THAT THE LITERATURE LACKS**
The mathematical work lives at He, Ne, two electrons, Z ≥ 35. **We have 107 neutral atoms across the whole physical range with the deciding quantity measured at every one** — margins, runner-up identities, candidate-set sizes. That is a map of the object over the domain the theorems cannot reach.

**§3 · AND THE LEMMA THAT WOULD HAVE CLOSED IT IS FALSIFIED — BY OUR OWN DATA**
I drafted the obvious narrowing: *if the spread of reachable critical points is below half the argmin margin, non-uniqueness cannot change the answer.* Both numbers are measurable, so it looked closable.

I measured the spread. **`F76.2`: seed-to-seed margin disagreement reaches 35.58 mHa. The tightest chain margin is 32.330 mHa. The hypothesis fails.**

I also withdraw a lean I made two messages ago: the "0.005 mHa forgotten from 52 Ha away" figure is an **energy** agreement, not a **margin** agreement. I quoted it as evidence the critical point does not matter. It is not that evidence. Median margin disagreement across seeds is 1.95 mHa, and `ORDER_MATCH` holds at only 3 of 9 — **the ranking below the winner is not stable at all.**

`ENT_MATCH` is **9 of 9**. The entrant never moved, even where the margin moved by more than the tightest margin in the chain.

Three Z values, nine records. **Z=89 was never re-seeded.** The single measurement that would decide this has not been run. If the entrant flips at any seed at Z=89, the selection rule is load-bearing on the result and **Deliverable 1 inherits a dependency it does not currently declare.**

The Method 1.6 — The Register-1.md
** δ⁻¹({−1,+1}) is non-convex, has E = 750 and **E₄ = 0** — a non-convex set closed under the four-orientation operator. §17.3 is not weakened; it is **located**, and now names the operator it is about.

### 480

**The audits' two-cell orientation cost is one kind of audit.** Both cells ℛ admits and ℛ₄ refuses read *outside · dishonest · mutually inconsistent*, differing only in whether they read other places or a computation. They sit at the top of three coordinates at once, which an upward-only reading cannot refuse. **Two audits the structure admits and this book does not have** — and being refused by the tighter operator, the weaker kind of prediction.

### 481

**The seed is a bound and was reported as a value.** Greedy removal gives an upper bound: ℛ at 11, 12, 12, 13 across shuffles, ℛ₄ at 12, 15, 15, **overlapping**. §14.5.2's *eleven* is a greedy bound and now says so, and the prediction that ℛ₄ must need a larger seed is **neither confirmed nor refuted** — the variance swamps it. *An inconclusive result recorded as inconclusive, which §2.18 requires and which is easier to write than to remember to write.*

### 482

**The seed is constructible and need never be searched for.** ℛ(X) is determined by φ̂ alone, so the cells witnessing each envelope step — plus one per alphabet value — have the same envelopes and therefore the same closure. Verified at four cap settings. **|Λ| grows thirty-one-fold across them and the seed grows one-point-four-fold**, compression rising from 24× to **518×**, because the seed is bounded by O(d² × cap depth) and not by |Λ|.

### 483

**The seed is a size, not a set.** Six independent minimisations of Λ give six **distinct** seeds — 10, 10, 12, 12, 13, 13 — with **zero cells in common** and a union of 63. A convex geometry has one minimal generating set by anti-exchange; **anti-exchange fails here**, so ℛ's closed sets are a Moore family and not a convex geometry, and *the seed* names a cardinality rather than an object.

### 484

**No cell of Λ is removable and no cell is necessary.** Register 466 gives the first — ℛ(Λ \ {x}) = Λ for all 976 — and 483 gives the second. They are one fact: **Λ is maximally redundant in its own generators**, which is what makes a seed of ten possible and what makes it non-unique.

### 485

**The bound falls from eleven to ten.** Greedy across six shuffles reached ten twice, and the figure §14.5.2 carries is an upper bound in both directions of this session's reporting — it was written as a value, corrected to a bound, and has now moved.

### 486

**This book keeps two registers and had one word for them.** The **mathematics** register is a backlog — 47 unfinished of 152, and it shrinks as figures are verified. The **withdrawals** register is a closed index with a stable defect: measured at 248, 265 and 319 entries it gives **33 cells, 68.8% density and E = 6 every time.** Seventy-one entries and the shape has not moved.

The Method 1.6-1.md
D.4.4 Two perspectives of one definition, and one of them carries more
 F and ℛ are the same definition seen twice. F says what Λ contains; ℛ says what Λ requires. Both
 give 976 cells and neither is derived from the other's coupling.

 ℛ is idempotent. Λ → fifty-six recovered bounds → generates 976 → the same fifty-six bounds, and
 again the same. One application takes any presentation to a canonical form; further applications change
 nothing.

 The defining system is not that fixed point. F carries seven bounds; the normal form has sixteen
 that constrain, of fifty-six recovered. Both generate the same set.

 D.4.4.1 And three of the four directions are functions

  Λ → the recovered bounds                            unique — this is ℛ
  the recovered bounds → Λ                            unique — generate
  the defining bounds → Λ                             unique — this is Chapter 7
  Λ → the defining bounds                             NOT a function

 Many presentations give the same Λ. So ℛ forgets which one was used, and the forgetting is not
 recoverable.

    A presentation and its normal form are two perspectives of one definition, and the map
    between them runs one way.

 D.4.4.2 Which is what the single expression contributes
 F carries information Λ does not: the order in which the bounds were imposed.

 The caterpillar of Figure 6.1 — a path of seven nodes with one pendant at k — is a fact about
 the presentation, not about the set. §11.7 proves that a single closed expression exists because the
 constraint graph is a tree, and a tree is an ordering of impositions. Λ alone supplies no such order;
 §12.9 counts 1,113,045,672 maximal chains, and the construction picked one.

    That is why Chapter 11 and Chapter 15 are separate chapters. Chapter 11 needs the
    presentation. Chapter 15 recovers only what survives forgetting it.

 D.4.4.3 A refinement of P21
 P21 says a definition contained in the lattice is true in every language it can be written in. §11.1
 gives Λ in six, and the languages agree.

 They do not carry equal amounts. The generating-function perspective carries a nesting order the
 set-theoretic perspective does not, and the order is real — it determines whether a closed form exists at
 all.

    Every perspective on a contained definition is TRUE. They are not INTERCHANGEABLE. A
    perspective may carry structure the object does not, and a perspective that forgets it is still correct
    about the object.

 That is not a weakening of P21. It is the reason §11.7's proof has a hypothesis — the tree —
 which is a property of how Λ was written and not of what Λ is.

 D.5 The closed index
 With both constraints and both elements: E = 0 in all sixteen fibres, and **the theorem · order row
 carries the correction of §D.5.4** — five elements were printed here for years against a stated total
 of thirty-two, and the five that fit no row are A.4, A.5, A.11 and Chapter 16's two theorems.

The Method 1.6-1.md
** Prune-greedy — start from the witness set, drop while the closure still returns the index —
 is a poor set-cover algorithm, and every expression fitted to its output was fitted to its failures.

 **The definition exposed it.** §14.5.7 says G is a seed iff φ̂(G) = φ̂(X). Read as a covering
 problem — **elements are the envelope steps, sets are the cells, a cell covers the steps it
 witnesses** — the seed is a **minimum set cover**, and set cover has algorithms better than
 prune-greedy.

  object                cells   prune   cover  +prune  random  reverse   LB   **EXACT**   spread
  **Λ₈**                  976     12       7      7       7     **40**    5      **7**    **33**
  down-set d = 4, c = 4    35      7       7      7       7        7      7      **7**     **0**
  full box 3³              27      5       5      4       5        6      3      **4**       2
  full box 4³              64      6       6      5       6        8      4      **5**       3

    **seed(Λ₈) = 7, exactly, by branch and bound.** This book reported ten to thirteen
    for twelve cycles. **976 cells from seven — a compression of 139 to 1.**

 **And two laws become exact rather than fitted.** A down-set seeds at **d + c − 1** and a full box at
 **d + c − 2**, both confirmed by branch and bound, and the down-set's lower bound *equals* its upper
 bound. **Λ₈ seeds at 7 where d + c − 1 would give 11** — Λ is more constrained than a plain down-set
 and seeds more cheaply for it.

    **The spread across heuristics is the quantity to report.** Zero on the regular
    down-set, where every method agrees and the bound is tight. **Thirty-three on Λ₈**,
    where reverse-delete gives forty against an exact seven.

 **What this withdraws.** Registers 497 through 500 and 502 — that parent count drives seed cost at
 +10 against +1, that a two-parent axis costs a + 4, that cost = a + κ, that κ = S/4 − 1 at
 correlation +0.980, that the second variable is c. **Under a good heuristic a two-parent axis costs
 one or two cells, the same as a one-parent axis**, and refitting κ against S gives a coefficient of
 −0.079 at rms 0.999. **The parent-count effect was the heuristic's difficulty, not the index's
 cost**, and the correlation with S held because prune-greedy fails worse where the base is tighter.

 **What survives.** The definition. The set-cover reading. Linearity in d with slope one, now covering
 both families. The Carathéodory lower bound. seed(ℛ(X)) + E for open indexes. And **register 501's
 identity — the tight-pair count is exactly 2S** — which never depended on a seed measurement.

 Registers 503–506.

### 14.5.10 A stable core of four, and it is NOT necessary

 §14.5.7 records that **zero cells are forced**. **That is correct, and this section first said
 otherwise.**

 **Four cells appear in all 140 sampled seeds.

The Method 1.6 — The Register-1.md
**1493 entries, 165 to 1700.**

Every correction, withdrawal and finding in the order it happened. **The book cites entries where
they carry an argument; the complete record lives here.** Rebuild with `python3 register_gen.py >
REGISTER.md` — it reads the source, so it cannot drift.

**225 entries are cited somewhere in the book's chapters.** The rest
are the record of how the work went, which is the material §4's mechanisms were built from.

---

### 165

Fibre cardinality as an order seed. Proposed as a seed-independent break; fails to recover Λ's order.

### 166

"Closed under intersection, which a closure operator guarantees." Written while the output above it showed intersection failing in a quarter of pairs. The theorem does not apply because ℛ recovers its alphabet, so the ground set moves.

### 167

"A real limit on the self-reference claim." The union/intersection result is a fact about a superset of Λ. P22 concerns what an index contains. Completeness descends and does not ascend.

### 168

"A procedure." The monotone closure was called one when the closure contributes nothing — its fixed point leaves the relation empty, because the dual involution admits no unit clauses.

### 169

"The obstructions are larger in cells." The table said four of six had four or five cells and every one needed an alphabet of size 4. Small in cells, wide in alphabet — and then 170.

### 170

The alphabet reading itself. A k-cell instance has at most k values per axis. So the census is parameterised by cells alone, and 169's correction was also wrong in its conclusion.

### 171

"A real simplification." The identical-fibre quotient was measured on the subset where merging happens. Median reduction over all instances: 1.0×.

### 172

"They agree too much." Three cell statistics were called redundant. Separating joins from meets dropped their agreement to 33%, and a fourth statistic reached 94%.

### 173

"Fibre chains are sufficient." Exact at d = 2 — and violated at d ≥ 3 in 44 of 130 cases. The sufficient condition does not lift.

### 174

"Sublattices preserve reorderability, 100%." True for closing a seed under join and meet; false for deleting an arbitrary cell, which breaks it 20.5% of the time. One word covering two operations.

### 175

"Computable." Used to mean finite and well-defined. Λ's box has 10^2080 subsets. Both statements are true and they were run together. 176–177. Two generator failures, both on the recovered-versus-declared alphabet: a d = 2 census producing a third of the objects, and a d = 3 bound system that is both incomplete (281 against 319) and slower.

### 178

"d = 2 is closed." Written in the same message as "closure isn't the kind of thing that gets confirmed." By P23 the first should read: has survived every question asked of it.

### 179

"The hierarchy converges." Read off the d = 4 column while the d = 3 column was flat.

### 180

The sub-instance necessary condition. Recorded as "necessary, zero false negatives."
